# The Long Way Home: In Praise of Aimless Walking

At the end of the street, where the pavement gives way to gravel and the streetlights stop pretending to be stars, I turn left for no reason. This is the whole ritual. There is no destination, no step count to hit, no podcast in my ears. There is only the particular hush of a Tuesday evening in early autumn, the smell of wet leaves beginning their slow return to soil, and the strange, generous feeling of being unneeded by the world for an hour. It is in these walks that I remember something essential: that a human being is not a machine for output, but an animal built for drift.

I want to make a case for the aimless walk—not the exercise walk, not the mindfulness walk with its app-based breathing cues, not the walking meeting, but the walk that has no justification at all. The walk that meanders, doubles back, stops to look at a fence post or a crow or a crack in the sidewalk. The walk that would fail every productivity metric ever invented and is precisely valuable for that reason. In an age that wants every minute to be optimized, monetized, or documented, walking without purpose is a small act of rebellion. It is also, I have come to believe, one of the surest paths back to our own minds.

The history of walking is full of people who understood this. Jean-Jacques Rousseau claimed, “I can only meditate when I am walking. When I stop, I cease to think; my mind only works with my legs.” Søren Kierkegaard wrote that he had walked himself into his best thoughts and knew of no thought so burdensome that one could not walk away from it. Virginia Woolf used her long London walks to compose novels in her head, letting sentences rise and fall with her footsteps. Charles Dickens walked fifteen or twenty miles a night through the city, and the rhythm of his prose—urgent, observant, endlessly curious—seems to carry the gait of those nocturnal rambles. These were not people who walked for cardiovascular health, though they got that too. They walked because thinking and walking are not separate activities; they are two expressions of the same animal rhythm.

There is a reason for this. Modern neuroscience has begun to catch up with what philosophers and poets have known for centuries: that the brain is not a stationary engine that works best when the body is still. The brain is an organ of movement, evolved to navigate landscapes, to scan horizons, to respond to the changing sensory field of a moving body. When we walk, especially without a specific goal, the brain enters a state that researchers call the default mode network—a pattern of activity associated with daydreaming, memory consolidation, self-reflection, and the kind of loose, associative thinking that produces new ideas. This is not laziness. It is the mind doing its essential background work, the work of connection and synthesis that cannot be forced by focus alone.

Aimless walking, in other words, is not the absence of thought. It is thought’s natural habitat. When we walk without purpose, we give the mind permission to wander, and a wandering mind is often the one that stumbles upon the insight that a focused mind has been circling for days. The great mathematician Henri Poincaré described how he solved a difficult problem not at his desk but stepping onto a bus, his mind suddenly seeing the answer in a flash after he had set the work aside. The composer Gustav Mahler took long walks in the Alps and returned with symphonies in his head. The chemist August Kekulé dreamed of a snake eating its own tail and discovered the structure of benzene. These stories are usually told as examples of sudden genius, but they are equally stories of movement, of minds unclenched from their tasks, of bodies in motion giving thoughts room to breathe.

I have felt this in my own small way. On a walk last spring, I was not trying to solve anything. I was just walking, noticing the way the new leaves made the light look green and underwater, when a problem I had been wrestling with for weeks—a structural problem in a piece of writing, a knot I could not untie at my desk—simply loosened. The sentence I needed arrived not with a fanfare but with the casualness of a friend falling into step beside me. I had to stop on the sidewalk and write it down in the notes app on my phone, apologizing to a bush I had nearly walked into. This is not magic. It is just the way the mind works when we stop forcing it.

And yet we have built a world that makes this kind of walking feel almost illicit. The modern city is designed for efficiency, for getting from point A to point B as quickly as possible. Sidewalks are for transit, not for lingering. Benches are scarce, and the ones that exist are often designed to discourage sleeping or sitting too long. Public space is increasingly privatized, monitored, and optimized for consumption. The pedestrian is an obstacle to the flow of traffic, a lag in the system. To walk slowly, to stop and look at nothing, is to become a small anomaly in the urban machine. People might look at you with suspicion. What are you doing? Are you lost? Are you okay?

This suspicion reveals something about our cultural values. We have internalized the idea that time must be spent, not simply lived. We speak of “spending” time as if it were currency, and we feel guilty when we do not get a return on the investment. The aimless walk offers no return. It produces nothing. It cannot be optimized, tracked, or sold. It is radically unproductive. That is why it is so valuable. It is a reminder that there are modes of being that are not modes of production. It is a small, embodied refusal of the logic that says every hour must be accounted for.

The French have a word for the aimless urban walker: the flâneur. The flâneur emerged in nineteenth-century Paris as a figure who strolled through the arcades and boulevards, observing the city with a detached but passionate eye. Charles Baudelaire described the flâneur as “a prince who everywhere rejoices in his incognito,” a person who is at home in the crowd but never lost in it. Walter Benjamin later made the flâneur a central figure in his study of modern life, seeing in the aimless walker a kind of resistance to the acceleration of the city. The flâneur walks not to get somewhere but to be somewhere, to be present to the life of the streets, to let the city wash over him like weather.

The flâneur was always a somewhat privileged figure—usually male, usually leisured, usually able to walk without fear of harassment or violence. This privilege matters. The freedom to walk aimlessly is not equally distributed. Women, people of color, unhoused people, and others often do not have the luxury of being seen as harmless wanderers. A Black man walking slowly in a white neighborhood may be seen as a threat. A woman walking alone at night must calculate routes and risks. An unhoused person walking or sitting in public space is often criminalized for simply existing. Any honest defense of aimless walking must acknowledge these realities. The right to wander is a right that many are still fighting for, and the public space that makes wandering possible is a space that must be defended not just for some but for all.

Still, the ideal of the flâneur remains useful because it names a particular kind of attention. The flâneur is not just walking; he is looking. He is practicing what the poet Mary Oliver called “the first, wildest, and wisest thing”—attention. “Attention,” she wrote, “is the beginning of devotion.” To walk aimlessly is to practice attention without agenda. It is to look at the world not as a set of obstacles or resources but as a living tissue of detail and mystery. You notice the particular blue of a hydrant, the way the light pools in a gutter, the sound of a screen door closing three blocks away, the face of a stranger that contains a whole novel. This kind of attention is not productive, but it is nourishing. It feeds something in us that the engineered feeds of social media cannot reach.

I think often of the walks I took during the early months of the pandemic. The world had shrunk to the radius of a few blocks, and walking became a lifeline. I walked the same streets over and over, and the repetition taught me to see differently. The first time I walked them, I saw houses and trees and parked cars. By the tenth time, I saw the particular oak with the branch that looked like an elbow, the porch with the peeling white paint, the cat that always sat in the same window at the same hour. By the twentieth time, I felt a kind of intimacy with the neighborhood, a sense that I was walking through a landscape that was also a relationship. The streets had become not just a route but a place. I was paying attention, and attention had turned the ordinary into something almost sacred.

This is the quiet gift of the aimless walk: it teaches you to love where you are. Not some idealized version of nature or some exotic destination, but the actual ground beneath your feet. The gutter, the sidewalk crack, the dandelion pushing through concrete, the smell of rain on asphalt, the sound of your own breathing. In a culture that is constantly telling us to be elsewhere—to travel, to upgrade, to escape—the aimless walk is a practice of staying. It says: here is enough. This ordinary world, with its weeds and wires and weather, is enough to hold your attention for an hour, and if you let it, it will hold your attention for a lifetime.

There is also something deeply democratic about walking. You don’t need money to walk. You don’t need a membership or a subscription or a special outfit. You just need a body and a bit of ground. Walking is one of the oldest human activities, older than language, older than tools, older than civilization. Our ancestors walked out of Africa and across continents. They walked to hunt, to gather, to migrate, to explore. Walking is in our bones, and when we walk, we are participating in a lineage that stretches back millions of years. This is not mystical; it is just the truth of our evolutionary history. We are animals whose minds were shaped by movement, and we forget this at our peril.

In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in walking. Books about walking have become bestsellers. Podcasts about walking are popular. People are rediscovering the simple act of putting one foot in front of the other as a remedy for the disconnection of modern life. This is good, but I worry that walking is being turned into another form of self-improvement, another item on the to-do list. We are told to walk for our mental health, for our creativity, for our longevity. These are real benefits, but they can also become another way of instrumentalizing the walk, of making it serve a purpose. The deepest value of the aimless walk is that it has no purpose. It is an end in itself. It is a small, defiant assertion that some things matter without needing to matter for anything.

I am not naive. I know that an aimless walk will not solve the climate crisis or end inequality or heal the wounds of history. But I also know that the world is made of small practices, and small practices shape the kind of people we become. A person who walks without purpose is a person who has learned to be patient with not knowing. A person who stops to look at a tree is a person who has practiced reverence for what they did not plan to see. A person who wanders without a map is a person who has made peace with the possibility of getting lost. These are not small things. They are the habits of mind that make us more humane, more curious, more open to the unexpected. They are the antidote to a world that wants us to be predictable, efficient, and always moving in a straight line.

So here is my invitation. Step outside. Leave your phone at home, or at least put it in your pocket. Do not choose a destination. Do not set a timer. Just walk. When you reach a corner, flip a coin in your head. Let the streetlights and the weather and the movement of your own body decide. Notice what you notice. Stop when something asks you to stop. There is no wrong way to do this. The only failure is to turn it into a task.

I took one of these walks just yesterday. The sky was the color of a bruise, purple and yellow at the edges, and the air smelled like woodsmoke and rain. I walked past a house where someone was practicing piano, the notes spilling out of an open window and dissolving into the evening. I passed a man walking a small dog who was very proud of a stick. I passed a yard where a child had left a red plastic truck on its side, and the image of that truck—small, abandoned, bright against the green grass—stayed with me for blocks. I had no thoughts worth writing down. I had no revelations. I just walked, and the world walked with me, and for an hour I was not a person with tasks and worries and a calendar full of obligations. I was just a body moving through the world, and that was enough.

The French philosopher Frédéric Gros, in his book *A Philosophy of Walking*, writes: “Walking is sport without a winner, leisure without consumption, a way of being in the world without having anything to do.” I think of this line often. It names the strange liberty of the walk. In a culture of winners and consumers and doers, the walker is none of these things. The walker is a witness, a guest, a pair of eyes. The walker is someone who has temporarily stepped out of the race. And the race, of course, will be there when they return. The emails will still be waiting. The news will still be terrible. The world will still demand its due. But for a little while, the walker has been free.

This freedom is not an escape from the world; it is a deeper entrance into it. The walker is not fleeing reality but embracing it at the speed of a human body. The walker feels the ground beneath their feet, the wind on their skin, the ache in their knees. They hear the birds and the traffic and the distant siren. They see the litter and the flowers and the graffiti. They are not above the world or outside it; they are in it, moving through it, part of its messy, beautiful, heartbreaking texture. This is what the aimless walk offers: not a way out, but a way in.

In the end, the case for aimless walking is not a case against purpose. It is a case for the spaciousness that purpose needs in order to breathe. The musician needs silence between notes. The painter needs empty canvas. The thinker needs empty time. Without the fallow, there is no fruit. Without the rest, there is no work. Without the walk that goes nowhere, there is no arrival that means anything. So walk. Not to get somewhere. Just to be somewhere, moving. The long way home may turn out to be the way home after all.

The great mathematician Henri Poincaré described how he solved a difficult problem not at his desk but stepping onto a bus, his mind suddenly seeing the answer in a flash after he had set the work aside. The composer Gustav Mahler took long walks in the Alps and returned with symphonies in his head. The chemist August Kekulé dreamed of a snake eating its own tail and discovered the structure of benzene. These stories are usually told as examples of sudden genius, but they are equally stories of movement, of minds unclenched from their tasks, of bodies in motion giving thoughts room to breathe.

I have felt this in my own small way. On a walk last spring, I was not trying to solve anything. I was just walking, noticing the way the new leaves made the light look green and underwater, when a problem I had been wrestling with for weeks—a structural problem in a piece of writing, a knot I could not untie at my desk—simply loosened. The sentence I needed arrived not with a fanfare but with the casualness of a friend falling into step beside me. I had to stop on the sidewalk and write it down in the notes app on my phone, apologizing to a bush I had nearly walked into. This is not magic. It is just the way the mind works when we stop forcing it.

And yet we have built a world that makes this kind of walking feel almost illicit. The modern city is designed for efficiency, for getting from point A to point B as quickly as possible. Sidewalks are for transit, not for lingering. Benches are scarce, and the ones that exist are often designed to discourage sleeping or sitting too long. Public space is increasingly privatized, monitored, and optimized for consumption. The pedestrian is an obstacle to the flow of traffic, a lag in the system. To walk slowly, to stop and look at nothing, is to become a small anomaly in the urban machine. People might look at you with suspicion. What are you doing? Are you lost? Are you okay?

This suspicion reveals something about our cultural values. We have internalized the idea that time must be spent, not simply lived. We speak of “spending” time as if it were currency, and we feel guilty when we do not get a return on the investment. The aimless walk offers no return. It produces nothing. It cannot be optimized, tracked, or sold. It is radically unproductive. That is why it is so valuable. It is a reminder that there are modes of being that are not modes of production. It is a small, embodied refusal of the logic that says every hour must be accounted for.

The French have a word for the aimless urban walker: the flâneur. The flâneur emerged in nineteenth-century Paris as a figure who strolled through the arcades and boulevards, observing the city with a detached but passionate eye. Charles Baudelaire described the flâneur as “a prince who everywhere rejoices in his incognito,” a person who is at home in the crowd but never lost in it. Walter Benjamin later made the flâneur a central figure in his study of modern life, seeing in the aimless walker a kind of resistance to the acceleration of the city. The flâneur walks not to get somewhere but to be somewhere, to be present to the life of the streets, to let the city wash over him like weather.

The flâneur was always a somewhat privileged figure—usually male, usually leisured, usually able to walk without fear of harassment or violence. This privilege matters. The freedom to walk aimlessly is not equally distributed. Women, people of color, unhoused people, and others often do not have the luxury of being seen as harmless wanderers. A Black man walking slowly in a white neighborhood may be seen as a threat. A woman walking alone at night must calculate routes and risks. An unhoused person walking or sitting in public space is often criminalized for simply existing. Any honest defense of aimless walking must acknowledge these realities. The right to wander is a right that many are still fighting for, and the public space that makes wandering possible is a space that must be defended not just for some but for all.

Still, the ideal of the flâneur remains useful because it names a particular kind of attention. The flâneur is not just walking; he is looking. He is practicing what the poet Mary Oliver called “the first, wildest, and wisest thing”—attention. “Attention,” she wrote, “is the beginning of devotion.” To walk aimlessly is to practice attention without agenda. It is to look at the world not as a set of obstacles or resources but as a living tissue of detail and mystery. You notice the particular blue of a hydrant, the way the light pools in a gutter, the sound of a screen door closing three blocks away, the face of a stranger that contains a whole novel. This kind of attention is not productive, but it is nourishing. It feeds something in us that the engineered feeds of social media cannot reach.

I think often of the walks I took during the early months of the pandemic. The world had shrunk to the radius of a few blocks, and walking became a lifeline. I walked the same streets over and over, and the repetition taught me to see differently. The first time I walked them, I saw houses and trees and parked cars. By the tenth time, I saw the particular oak with the branch that looked like an elbow, the porch with the peeling white paint, the cat that always sat in the same window at the same hour. By the twentieth time, I felt a kind of intimacy with the neighborhood, a sense that I was walking through a landscape that was also a relationship. The streets had become not just a route but a place. I was paying attention, and attention had turned the ordinary into something almost sacred.

This is the quiet gift of the aimless walk: it teaches you to love where you are. Not some idealized version of nature or some exotic destination, but the actual ground beneath your feet. The gutter, the sidewalk crack, the dandelion pushing through concrete, the smell of rain on asphalt, the sound of your own breathing. In a culture that is constantly telling us to be elsewhere—to travel, to upgrade, to escape—the aimless walk is a practice of staying. It says: here is enough. This ordinary world, with its weeds and wires and weather, is enough to hold your attention for an hour, and if you let it, it will hold your attention for a lifetime.

There is also something deeply democratic about walking. You don’t need money to walk. You don’t need a membership or a subscription or a special outfit. You just need a body and a bit of ground. Walking is one of the oldest human activities, older than language, older than tools, older than civilization. Our ancestors walked out of Africa and across continents. They walked to hunt, to gather, to migrate, to explore. Walking is in our bones, and when we walk, we are participating in a lineage that stretches back millions of years. This is not mystical; it is just the truth of our evolutionary history. We are animals whose minds were shaped by movement, and we forget this at our peril.

In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in walking. Books about walking have become bestsellers. Podcasts about walking are popular. People are rediscovering the simple act of putting one foot in front of the other as a remedy for the disconnection of modern life. This is good, but I worry that walking is being turned into another form of self-improvement, another item on the to-do list. We are told to walk for our mental health, for our creativity, for our longevity. These are real benefits, but they can also become another way of instrumentalizing the walk, of making it serve a purpose. The deepest value of the aimless walk is that it has no purpose. It is an end in itself. It is a small, defiant assertion that some things matter without needing to matter for anything.

I am not naive. I know that an aimless walk will not solve the climate crisis or end inequality or heal the wounds of history. But I also know that the world is made of small practices, and small practices shape the kind of people we become. A person who walks without purpose is a person who has learned to be patient with not knowing. A person who stops to look at a tree is a person who has practiced reverence for what they did not plan to see. A person who wanders without a map is a person who has made peace with the possibility of getting lost. These are not small things. They are the habits of mind that make us more humane, more curious, more open to the unexpected. They are the antidote to a world that wants us to be predictable, efficient, and always moving in a straight line.

So here is my invitation. Step outside. Leave your phone at home, or at least put it in your pocket. Do not choose a destination. Do not set a timer. Just walk. When you reach a corner, flip a coin in your head. Let the streetlights and the weather and the movement of your own body decide. Notice what you notice. Stop when something asks you to stop. There is no wrong way to do this. The only failure is to turn it into a task.

I took one of these walks just yesterday. The sky was the color of a bruise, purple and yellow at the edges, and the air smelled like woodsmoke and rain. I walked past a house where someone was practicing piano, the notes spilling out of an open window and dissolving into the evening. I passed a man walking a small dog who was very proud of a stick. I passed a yard where a child had left a red plastic truck on its side, and the image of that truck—small, abandoned, bright against the green grass—stayed with me for blocks. I had no thoughts worth writing down. I had no revelations. I just walked, and the world walked with me, and for an hour I was not a person with tasks and worries and a calendar full of obligations. I was just a body moving through the world, and that was enough.

The French philosopher Frédéric Gros, in his book *A Philosophy of Walking*, writes: “Walking is sport without a winner, leisure without consumption, a way of being in the world without having anything to do.” I think of this line often. It names the strange liberty of the walk. In a culture of winners and consumers and doers, the walker is none of these things. The walker is a witness, a guest, a pair of eyes. The walker is someone who has temporarily stepped out of the race. And the race, of course, will be there when they return. The emails will still be waiting. The news will still be terrible. The world will still demand its due. But for a little while, the walker has been free.

This freedom is not an escape from the world; it is a deeper entrance into it. The walker is not fleeing reality but embracing it at the speed of a human body. The walker feels the ground beneath their feet, the wind on their skin, the ache in their knees. They hear the birds and the traffic and the distant siren. They see the litter and the flowers and the graffiti. They are not above the world or outside it; they are in it, moving through it, part of its messy, beautiful, heartbreaking texture. This is what the aimless walk offers: not a way out, but a way in.

In the end, the case for aimless walking is not a case against purpose. It is a case for the spaciousness that purpose needs in order to breathe. The musician needs silence between notes. The painter needs empty canvas. The thinker needs empty time. Without the fallow, there is no fruit. Without the rest, there is no work. Without the walk that goes nowhere, there is no arrival that means anything. So walk. Not to get somewhere. Just to be somewhere, moving. The long way home may turn out to be the way home after all.
